newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: World's first euthanasia law could be killed off.
newsitem.headline: World's first euthanasia law could be killed off.

text.p: The world's only voluntary euthanasia law is looking terminally ill.
In fact, both supporters and opponents of euthanasia believe the law will be killed off by Australia's parliament within the next two weeks -- although the vote will be close.
Debate on a private member's bill aimed at overturning the law begins in the upper house Senate on Tuesday. A final conscience vote is expected a few days after that.

Politicians in the Australian parliament's lower house have already voted overwhelmingly to repeal the outback Northern Territory's euthanasia law, which came into effect in July 1996 and has since seen four people end their lives.
If the law is overturned, the move will be made in the face of polls showing 75 percent of Australians support euthanasia.

Euthanasia supporters believe they have lost their fight because the euthanasia debate is not simply an important moral question -- which is why politicians are being given a conscience vote -- but a political minefield.

They argue that religious MPs have hijacked the issue and that Australia's conservative government, which relies on the vote of two key independents, one of whom is a devout Catholic, has fallen into line.
In a rare show of support by the major parties for a private member's bill, both government and opposition leaders publicly supported the anti-euthanasia bill before the lower house vote.
"I think there have got to be some absolutes in life, and respect for human life is one of those," Australian Prime Minister John Howard told parliament at the time.
"I know that's not a popular view of a lot of people if you read the polls, but that's my personal view," Howard said.

Dr Robert Marr from the Coalition of Organisations for Voluntary Euthanasia believes the prime minister and other political leaders should have remained silent prior to the vote, allowing politicians a true conscience vote.
"It is absolutely outrageous that a handful of religious fanatics in parliament have been able to push this bill whereby it may well overturn the law," Marr told Reuters.
The Vatican has condemned the law as a "revolt against God, author of life, and a crime against life".
For the past year the euthanasia fight has been waged across Australia -- on city streets, in parliaments, in courts, in outback Aboriginal camps and even on Internet sites.
Aborigines are generally opposed to euthanasia, fearing it is a form of sorcery. Doctors say many ill Aborigines could simply avoid life-saving treatment if the law is maintained.
The "Deliverance" homepage announces the latest euthanasia death and has a simulation of the computer death machine and programme used to help four terminally ill people die.
In response, anti-euthanasia groups created their own Web-site -- "Living in Australia Without Deadly Deliverance".
Both camps agree that unofficial euthanasia is widespread, with about 5,000 people dying with their doctors' help a year.
But pro-lifers argue that if euthanasia remains legal it will open the floodgates to killing. "It will start as a trickle and become a flood," said campaigner Margaret Tighe.
Counter-punching, Marr points out that only four people have used the law since September and that strict safeguards require three medical signatures before a person can use the law.
Marr believes national legal euthanasia will eventually arrive. South Australia state and the Australian Capital Territory have euthanasia bills before their parliaments.
Under Australia's constitution, the national parliament can override territory legislation, but not state laws.
"Australia is a democracy and when you have 75 percent of the people supporting voluntary euthanasia, eventually the politicians listen," Marr said.
